common_name: Luscious Bananarama Lantana (Compact Non-Fading Yellow Trailing Lantana)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost date in well-drained soil in full sun; Bananarama holds a steady bright yellow color rather than shifting through orange and red like standard Lantana camara, and its lower, more spreading habit suits hanging baskets and container edges as well as beds.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Luscious Bananarama is part of Proven Winners' Luscious lantana series, bred for a lower, more mounding and trailing habit than upright landscape lantana, with clear, consistent golden-yellow flower clusters held over the foliage from spring through frost without deadheading. Its compact size and spreading habit make it equally at home cascading from hanging baskets and containers or filling beds and borders, and like other modern lantana selections it is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, thriving through the hottest stretch of a Gulf South summer. The flowers are strong pollinator magnets, drawing butterflies and bees throughout the long bloom season. In zone 9 it typically dies back to the roots in a hard freeze but resprouts vigorously from a well-established root system.
sources: Proven Winners — Luscious lantana series notes

common_name: Tapien Verbena (Fine-Textured Mildew-Resistant Spreading Groundcover Verbena)

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in early spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9 Tapien performs best in the cooler shoulder seasons, since it can decline in the most humid, wet stretch of high summer.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, since good drainage and air movement are essential to keep this fine-textured verbena free of the powdery mildew that troubles older verbena selections in humid weather. Tapien is a vegetatively propagated groundcover verbena series bred in Japan for finely cut, almost fern-like foliage and a low, dense, fast-spreading habit that quickly carpets ground or spills over container edges in shades of blue, pink, violet, and white. Its improved mildew resistance compared to older verbena makes it noticeably more reliable through humid weather, though like most verbena it still prefers excellent drainage and dislikes soggy soil. Shear plants back by about a third if they become leggy in midsummer to refresh dense flowering, and expect the strongest performance during spring and fall in zone 9's mild-winter climate.
sources: Suntory Flowers — Tapien verbena series notes

common_name: Tukana Verbena (Vigorous Large-Flowered Spreading Landscape Verbena)

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in early spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Tukana's vigorous, fast-spreading habit covers ground quickly, making it useful for large beds, slopes, and mass plantings as well as containers.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants generously to allow room for this vigorous series to spread quickly. Tukana is a vegetatively propagated verbena series bred for larger flower clusters and stronger vigor than finer-textured groundcover verbena types, spreading rapidly to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat covered in color from spring through fall in shades of red, pink, purple, and white. Its rapid coverage makes it a practical choice for filling large sunny beds, slopes, and mass landscape plantings where quick, showy results matter, while good air circulation and well-drained soil keep it free of the powdery mildew that troubles older verbena in humid conditions. An occasional shearing back after a heavy flush of bloom keeps growth dense and encourages continued flowering through the season.
sources: Syngenta Flowers — Tukana verbena series notes

common_name: Intensia Phlox (Vigorous Heat-Tolerant Fragrant Annual Phlox Series)

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost into full sun in well-drained soil; Intensia was bred from Phlox drummondii crosses for much better heat and drought tolerance than older annual phlox, holding up through the peak of Gulf South summer once established.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and water deeply but infrequently once established to encourage the deep rooting that gives this series its notable drought tolerance. Intensia is a vegetatively propagated annual phlox series bred for a dense, mounded, well-branched habit covered in clusters of fragrant, brightly colored flowers that bloom continuously from spring through frost without deadheading. Its markedly improved heat and drought tolerance compared to older seed-grown annual phlox, along with good resistance to powdery mildew, makes it a far more reliable choice for hot, humid Gulf South summers where traditional phlox often struggles and fades. The mounded habit and long bloom season suit it well to beds, borders, and mixed containers, and light, regular feeding keeps the dense flower display going through the growing season.
sources: Proven Winners — Intensia phlox series notes

common_name: Rex Begonia Vine (Trailing Velvet-Leaved Vine with Iridescent Purple Foliage)

planting.note: Plant or move outdoors after the last frost into a warm, humid, shaded spot; this tender tropical vine is grown as a houseplant or hanging basket subject outside the tropics and must come indoors well before the first fall frost.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light or open shade with high humidity and consistently moist, well-drained soil, protecting the vine from direct sun and cold drafts, both of which cause leaf drop. Rex Begonia Vine is prized not for flowers but for its striking heart-shaped leaves, patterned in iridescent silver-green, deep purple, and burgundy on top with wine-red undersides, an unrelated tropical vine that despite the common name is a true Cissus rather than a begonia. Its twining, tendril-climbing stems trail attractively from hanging baskets or can be trained up a small trellis, making it a dramatic textural accent for shaded porches, sunrooms, or humid indoor spaces. It goes semi-dormant and may drop some leaves in winter's shorter days and drier air, resuming vigorous growth with warmth, humidity, and longer days in spring; regular misting or a pebble tray helps sustain the humidity it needs to look its best.
